newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Harsh conditions spark rash of Brazil prison riots.
newsitem.headline: Harsh conditions spark rash of Brazil prison riots.

text.p: Rebellions broke out in four Brazilian jails on Tuesday in the lastest wave of unrest to hit the South American country's notoriously overcrowded prison system.
Two of the revolts were in Sao Paulo state, where 56 prison riots have occurred this year, including seven in the past week alone, authorities said.
"We have a dramatic situation in public jails, police stations and detention centres," said Joao Benedito Azevedo Marques, head of the Sao Paulo state penitentiary system.

Crammed into cells, beaten by guards, frustrated by slow justice and robbed of food and clothing sent by relatives, Brazilian inmates have taken to rioting and hostage-taking to obtain better conditions and transfers to less crowded jails.

Prison violence is not new in Brazil. In October 1992, military police shot and killed 111 rioting inmates at Sao Paulo's Carandiru jail, Latin America's largest prison with more than 6,300 prisoners and 1,000 guards.
While recent riots have not been as violent, this year's years rash of prison rebellions is a sign of worsening conditions inside the facilities, according to experts.

Most of the rebellions ended without bloodshed within a day or two. But the victims are frequently prison workers, who are seized as hostages, and other inmates who are the victims of revenge by armed prisoners during the chaos of a riot.
Last week, three prisoners were killed by knife-wielding inmates when a riot broke out at Praia Grande prison after authorities foiled an escape bid by tunnel.

In another riot, inmates brandishing stilletos, hammers and skewers grabbed 10 guards at a prison in the southern city of Florianopolis. They were freed three days later after authorities transferred most inmates to other facilities.
The last nationwide prison census of 1995 said Brazilian jails housed 148,760 prisoners but were 72,000 beds short.
To cope, the government plans to build 44 new jails and spend $110 million to expand and refurbish existing ones.
Human rights activists say the situation in Brazil's prisons is explosive.
"They are time bombs," said James Cavallaro, director of U.S.-based Human Right Watch's Brazil office.
"They are all overcrowded and well below international standards. It doesn't take much to set them off," he added.
